# Bahrain rules out Iran meeting on Hormuz until diplomatic ties restored



Bahrain said on Saturday it would not attend any group meeting with Iran on the Strait of Hormuz until diplomatic relations between the two countries were restored, state media reported.

The Foreign Ministry said it had already conveyed the position to Oman, while stressing that any arrangement governing navigation through the strait should be based on international law and approved by the International Maritime Organization.

Bahrain also cited attacks on civilian and economic infrastructure, including the strike on Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, as a reason for its position.

# BRICS adopts declaration on war, sanctions and nuclear risks after Iran-UAE differences

BRICS leaders unanimously adopted a joint declaration on Saturday calling for diplomacy in international conflicts, opposing unilateral coercive measures and warning of growing nuclear risks, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said.

The declaration called for the peaceful resolution of disputes through “dialogue, consultation and diplomacy” and said nuclear safeguards, safety and security must be upheld even during armed conflicts. It also expressed concern over the growing risk of nuclear conflict.

The bloc condemned unilateral coercive measures that it said violated international law and voiced concern about tariffs and other trade restrictions inconsistent with World Trade Organization rules. It also encouraged further work on cross-border payments among BRICS countries.

Reuters had earlier reported that the declaration was expected to avoid naming individual countries as members worked to bridge differences between Iran and the United Arab Emirates over the regional war.

The agreement marks a shift from a BRICS foreign ministers' meeting in New Delhi in May, when differences between Tehran and Abu Dhabi prevented ministers from issuing a joint statement.

# Volodymyr Zelenskyy offers to meet Vladimir Putin at G20 summit in Miami

In an interview with DW, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was in a strong position to negotiate and offered to meet Vladimir Putin.

A file picture of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. (Photo: Genya Savilov/ AFP)

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he would travel to Miami if his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, attended the Group of 20 (G20) leaders' summit scheduled for December.

Zelenskyy replied enthusiastically when DW's correspondent Misha Komadovsky posed the question on Friday. "Yes, of course. We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions," he said.

Zelenskyy added that what he was going to say to Putin mattered less than results. "It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. [...] Results matter. That's it."

## More To Read

Zelenskyy and Putin have not met in person since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its smaller neighbour in February 2022.

The Kremlin has so far declined to say whether Putin would go to Miami for the meeting. The Russian leader has not personally attended a G20 summit since 2019.

Last month, Russia's Finance Minister Anton Siluanov was, however, invited by the US to attend a meeting of G20 countries in North Carolina in a move that upset European officials.

# Zelenskyy warns Russia of retaliation if it targets Ukraine’s energy system this winter

## - ‘If they cause blackouts for us, we will try to respond in fitting fashion,’ Ukrainian president says

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday warned Russia would face retaliation if it targets Ukraine’s energy system this winter.

“Russia knows that if they strike – and they are preparing to strike our energy system this winter – Russia will receive the same in return,” Zelenskyy wrote on US social media platform X. “If they cause blackouts for us, we will try to respond in fitting fashion.”

Zelenskyy said negotiations remain Ukraine’s preferred path to ending the war.

He called for progress toward a possible trilateral meeting involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States, establishing an energy truce, the unblocking of the Black Sea, and continued exchanges of prisoners and civilians, including children held in Russia.

Zelenskyy warned that prolonging the war poses challenges to Russia and the global economy, particularly for food and energy security, and said disruptions to Black Sea grain exports could worsen shortages in vulnerable countries.

“This will be like Hormuz, only agricultural. And that is a serious problem. It shouldn’t be up to Ukraine alone to solve this. Because it is a challenge for many,” he said.

Zelenskyy also called for Congress to pass sanctions legislation backed by late Sen. Lindsey Graham and urged stronger action by the administration

China's Ministry of Commerce formally threatened legal action against American companies operating on Chinese soil on Friday, invoking the Counter-Espionage Law as its retaliatory instrument of choice — a direct response to CIA Deputy Director Michael Ellis's public declaration last week that Chinese companies in artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and biotechnology are now legitimate CIA intelligence targets. The ministry formally invoked espionage law powers against American companies, marking one of Beijing's most direct responses to a US intelligence declaration in years. The confrontation arrives with the September 24 White House summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping twelve days away, adding a sharp intelligence-community dimension to an already complicated diplomatic agenda.

Ellis made the declaration at the Billington Cybersecurity Summit in Washington on Tuesday, September 8, in remarks that were unusually direct for a serving intelligence official. The Federal News Network covered his Billington remarks directly. The core argument he advanced is structural: because China does not have a genuinely independent private sector — the Communist Party can absorb or direct any Chinese company at will — commercial Chinese firms in strategically important industries are not meaningfully different from state actors for intelligence purposes.

# Donald Trump talked about a united Ireland in Dublin, not the September 29 pharma deadline

[![Vipul Sipani](/byline-avatar?src=%2Fuploads%2Fmedia%2F1784007549648-6t66ua-548213531-10223333460643628-9176988883533667581-n.webp)](/trade-policy/author/vipul/)

[By Vipul Sipani](/trade-policy/author/vipul/)

4 min read·Published on Sep 13, 2026 · 12:08 AM IST

## Key takeaways

* Donald Trump arrived in Dublin on Saturday, September 12, and said Irish reunification "would be a fantastic thing." He said the leaders planned to discuss trade and tariffs, but nothing public emerged on the pharmaceutical tariff facing Ireland's largest export sector.
* Smaller pharmaceutical exporters without a US agreement reach their Section 232 compliance deadline on September 29 — seventeen days after the visit.
* Pharmaceutical products were €82bn of Ireland's €117.7bn exports to the United States in 2025, and 53% of all Irish exports. US multinationals employ about 11% of Irish workers.
* The fourteen largest manufacturers already hold 0% exemptions through January 20, 2029. The tariff lands on the firms that had no leverage to negotiate one.
